answer: A significant challenge facing young people today is the immense pressure created by social media. In my view, constant exposure to carefully curated, idealised versions of other people's lives has become genuinely [[detrimental]] to mental health. Everyone seems to be on holiday, getting engaged or landing a dream job, and it is easy to forget that these are just the highlights. This exists because platforms are designed to be [[addictive]], encouraging endless comparison. The more time we spend scrolling, the more money these companies make, so they have little reason to change. It affects almost all young people, who often feel inadequate when measuring their real lives against these unrealistic highlights. I see it in my younger sister's friends, who worry about how many likes a photo gets, and in some of the students I advise, who compare themselves with classmates who have already gone abroad. I think it can lead to serious anxiety and a distorted sense of self-worth. To tackle it, I believe we need better education about using social media [[mindfully]], along with a cultural shift towards valuing authenticity over appearances. Parents and teachers also need to talk about it openly, rather than simply banning phones. Honestly, I think the platforms themselves should also [[bear some responsibility]] for their design. It is a complex issue without a simple solution. Having grown up alongside this technology, I have felt its effects personally. I think raising awareness is the crucial first step, helping young people understand that what they see online is rarely the full, honest picture, and that real life is far more [[nuanced]].

followUps.q: Do you think this problem is worse for girls or boys?
followUps.answer: It affects both, but perhaps differently. Girls often face more pressure about appearance, while boys feel pressure to look successful or wealthy. Neither is healthy, and both deserve more attention.

followUps.q: Would you ever give up social media completely?
followUps.answer: Probably not, because I use it to stay in touch with family and for work. But I have become far more [[selective]], unfollowing accounts that make me feel worse rather than better.

note: Added why platforms keep it this way, examples from his sister's friends and students he advises, and a role for parents and teachers; plain-ish 'responsibility' widened to [[bear some responsibility]], added [[nuanced]].
